column2: Is the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation planning construction of a radio-television centre in the city of Montreal and in the city of Toronto?
If so, how much land is being purchased for the centres in Montreal and Toronto; and will such property be located in the downtown area or in the suburbs?
What is the market value of the property to be purchased in Montreal and Toronto?
What are the main requirements for locating a radio-television centre for C.B.C. operations?
Is the corporation planning to build a centre in Vancouver on its property on Georgia street or elsewhere in Vancouver?
What is the recommended acreage required for C.B.C. operations in Vancouver?

Lambert (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue):,Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue,STARRED QUESTIONS,C.B.C. CENTRES, MONTREAL-TORONTO-VANCOUVER",,"This is a six part question, and I will answer accordingly, I am informed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as follows:

column2: Yes.

33 acres of land have been purchased in suburban metropolitan Toronto. The area required for a Montreal consolidation site will be generally of the same order but precise areas cannot be determined until specific sites have been examined in detail.
The Toronto site was purchased for the sum of $635,000 serviced. No decision has been made as to Montreal.
Among other factors are:
Acceptability from a technical standpoint.
Sufficient area to permit the most economical construction of the known requirements together with provision for future developments.
Accessibility by public and private transportation during the full operating day together with adequate parking facilities.
Protection from present and future development which would be undesirable from a technical and administrative standpoint.
Consideration has been given to this in connection with the long range plans for development of the corporation.
When a decision is made the acreage will depend on the factors set out in No. 2 above.

column2: Has the Minister of National Defence in the past two years made any public statement on his department's intentions with regard to providing military personnel with training at forest firefighting, and of the availability of such a forest fire force for emergency situations in the country?
If so, when and where?
How many men have been trained to take part in forest firefighting in the past two years?
What liaison and training facilities were developed with provincial forest firefighting services?
In the summer of 1961, how was such a military force deployed to meet the forest fire crisis in British Columbia. Manitoba. Ontario, and Newfoundland?

,New Democratic Party,,Mr. Fisher,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=6e0e7dad-52e6-426d-b6d7-f3a4924ce2de&Language=E&Section=ALL
2140384,ca.proc.d.1961-09-13.1.3.2,1961-09-13,1351065a-17a8-47d3-af29-a838f6216a9c,ca.m.9588,Mr. Egan Chambers (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence):,Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence,STARRED QUESTIONS,FOREST FIREFIGHTING ASSISTANCE, NATIONAL DEFENCE",,"1.
column2: No.
Not applicable.
28,319 regular army soldiers received individual training in forest fire suppression during the past two years either during recruit training or during annual refresher training.

Approximately 485 officers and men participated in forest firefighting training conducted in conjunction with or by provincial forestry officials. This training took the form of liaison visits, reconnaissance or planning activities and attendance by army personnel at courses, lectures or demonstrations conducted by provincial officials.
British Columbia, no assistance was requested; Manitoba, 595 officers and men; Ontario, 14 officers and men; Newfoundland, 1,100 officers and men.

,Liberal Labour,,Mr. Benidickson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=52856d3c-42ed-4a84-9d56-17dfff0a98d5&Language=E&Section=ALL

answer is as follows. Permits issued by the wheat board for the import of oats from the United States are valid for a period of one month. There is no assurance that a permit issued to an importing firm will be filled in whole or in part. Since the release of details with respect to permits issued may imply a greater volume of imports than actually takes place, it is not considered in the public interest to reveal details which may not reflect actual import volumes and which might be detrimental to the board in its marketing operations in the commodity concerned. The import permits cover quantities only and do not stipulate prices.

column2: Yes.

The Canadian wheat board concluded a further sale of wheat to China under the long term agreement negotiated last April. 2140445,ca.proc.d.1961-09-13.16.1.8,1961-09-13,6dec82d6-fab3-438b-b40f-c7720a93d8c1,ca.m.5451,Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):,Secretary of State for External Affairs,UNITED NATIONS,REPORTED CONFLICT IN KATANGA,,Mr. Speaker, it is quite obvious that my interview with the foreign minister of Iceland did not last long enough.

It has been evident for several days now that a very tense situation was building up in Katanga, with the prospect that the United Nations might have to take firm measures to forestall the outbreak of large scale violence. While we do not yet have official reports on the latest developments, it would appear that the UN command now has moved to bring and keep the situation under control.

As hon. members are aware, there has been acute political tension in the Congo over the question of reintegrating the province of Katanga into the republic. One aspect of the resistance by some Katanga political leaders against a reconciliation with the central government appears to have been the revival of intertribal conflict in Katanga where, as the house will recall, there were heavy casualties in tribal clashes before the UN forces became established in that area.

One of the principal obligations imposed upon the United Nations command by the security council resolution of last February 21 was ""to prevent the occurrence of civil war"" in the Congo, and this was to include the prevention of armed clashes. The resolution specified that the measures which the United Nations might take in pursuit of this prime objective of preventing civil conflict should include the use of force ""if necessary, in the last resort"".

It is evidently the assessment of the United Nations authorities concerned that the situation in Katanga has now deteriorated to the point where strong measures offer the best likelihood of averting much more serious violence. Undoubtedly this decision is closely related to the recent reports that many thousands of Baluba tribesmen have sought United Nation protection in the face of reviving intertribal fighting. It is our earnest hope that by the present measures the United Nations will succeed in heading off more widespread trouble.
As far as we are aware, no Canadian personnel in the Congo have been involved in the current clashes in Katanga. There is one Canadian liaison officer with the UN units
Inquiries of the Ministry in Elizabethville. We expect to be having reports, of course, and when they are available I shall be very glad to inform the house.

Michael Starr (Minister of Labour):,Minister of Labour,LABOUR CONDITIONS,RECRUITMENT OF CANADIANS FOR U.K. GROCERY CHAIN,,I read in the newspaper this morning the article indicating that Loblaw Groceterias Company Limited were advertising for 500 Canadians for jobs in their stores in Great Britain.

I immediately got in touch with Mr. George C. Metcalf of the Loblaw company, who informed me that the only reason for this recruitment of Canadians is that this company is in the process of opening up 40 new stores in Great Britain in the immediate future. This company finds that there is a great lack of experience in the supermarket business in Great Britain. Consequently they are unable to recruit the type of help to which they are accustomed in the efficient operation of their stores. Their experience is that Canadians have been exposed to the supermarkets in Canada for a great many years and are easily integrated into that type of business.

I am also informed that Mr. Weston, who prides himself on being a Canadian and who knows Canadian characteristics, is anxious to have Canadians man these stores, in order to carry on an efficient business in Great Britain.
In view of this consideration, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who asked the question is putting a wrong interpretation on the whole situation.

Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):,Prime Minister,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,ANNOUNCEMENT OF VISIT BY PRIME MINISTER,,Mr. Speaker, an announcement was made yesterday in Tokyo to the effect that, following two invitations given to me to visit Japan, one by Prime Minister Kishi and the other by Prime Minister Ikeda, to which reference was made in the communique issued on the occasion of the visit of Mr. Ikeda, I had accepted.
These plans were made some time ago. The acceptance has been given. I point out

to the house that this of course is subject to intervening events. My visit will cover the last five days of October. We have tremendous trade relations with Japan and in the matter of world events concerning freedom Japan occupies a prominent place.

The last visit by a Canadian prime minister was by Mr. St. Laurent in 1954, and it brought benefits to Canada. I have found, and I think this view is generally shared by the leaders of the various countries, that these visits have a pronounced beneficial effect and are necessary. I know that if there is nothing during the intervening period which prevents my visiting there for that number of days, my visit will not only repay the visits made to this country but will strengthen our relationship with Japan and also lead, as Prime Minister Ikeda has said, to an extension of our trade relations.

2140472,ca.proc.d.1961-09-13.20.2.5,1961-09-13,bd7064c6-90b2-4e0a-9a8f-1c4d781bb30e,ca.m.4192,Mr. Fulton:,Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE INQUIRY AS TO MEETING TO AMEND CONSTITUTION,,The conference of attorneys general reached a very encouraging degree of agreement on the outstanding problems between us. As was stated in the official communique issued at the end of the meeting, most of the discussion concerned the question of a formula for the delegation of power as between the dominion parliament and provincial legislatures. This was the main point upon which agreement had not been reached in earlier discussions. Most of our discussions in the last two days were devoted to trying to arrive at agreement in principle on this matter. In this we were largely successful.

The position now is that the draftsmen assisting us have been instructed to prepare a final draft of all the proposals which have been discussed and upon which agreement has been reached. When that is done it will be placed in final form before the attorneys general for submission to and consideration by their governments. It is the hope that the
governments will find it possible to accept this as a basis for proposals to lay before their respective legislatures.

If that should be the case, then the work of the attorneys general conference is concluded. If, however, differences of substance emerge in the course of consideration by governments it may be necessary to reconvene the attorneys general conference in a further effort to reconcile points of difference.

I would also advise the house that at the time the final draft is placed in the hands of the attorneys general for them in turn to place before their governments, the text of our recommendation will be made public.

,Progressive Conservative,,Edmund Davie Fulton,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=bd7064c6-90b2-4e0a-9a8f-1c4d781bb30e&Language=E&Section=ALL

Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):,Prime Minister,PRIVY COUNCIL,,,"Mr. Chairman, the one item with which I will deal at this moment will be the emergency measures and the organization in general, in order to place before the committee some indication of the measures that have been taken for survival. I take it

Supply-Privy Council that this will provide the committee with an opportunity to hear the views of various members regarding this matter. I trust that after discussion general support will be given to the measures and plans which have been evolved and are in effect.

The committee started with a consideration of external affairs and proceeded to a general discussion of the problem of defence. As indicated by me the other day, I hoped for an early opportunity to place before the committee something of the views of the government in the application of the principles of survival as developed by co-operation among federal, provincial, and municipal authorities.

On September 7, the Minister of National Defence and I made statements to the house regarding decisions that had been made on certain emergency preparations in the defence field. At that time I indicated that I would make a more comprehensive statement on emergency measures. I am not going to repeat any of the matters or deal with the questions that were dealt with earlier, except to say that the progress made by the Department of National Defence in respect of the order in council for emergency planning passed in 1959 which has resulted in the formulation of plans that can be brought rapidly into action at a time of crisis is in the opinion of the government confirmation of the wisdom of the decision that was made to assign to the Department of National Defence certain major responsibilities in the emergency planning field.

The statement made by the Minister of National Defence on September 7 dealt more particularly with the national survival role of that department. I wish at this time to say something further with respect to other aspects of emergency planning as they affect the public in general.

Two matters are very much in the minds of the Canadian people at the moment. One is that at a time of stress and difficulty, with the ever-increasing threats made by Mr. Khrushchev and the increasing number of explosions of larger and larger instruments of destruction, the people are asking what are the possibilities of evacuation or dispersal of residents of larger urban centres, and in particular those that are probable target areas. The other question is the matter of individual shelter, what can be done to provide helpful and meaningful action to reduce the number of persons who would die in any area should such an event take place, and in particular in large cities.

Some say that action in this regard will be ineffective. That is not the point of view of those who know and have given study to this matter not only in our country but in the United Kingdom, the United States and other

Supply-Privy Council countries. Indeed, without going into detail at the moment, may I say this. According to the recent announcement of the President of the United States on this important matter, a number of those things which we in Canada had adopted earlier have been accepted now in that country as important steps toward survival. A certain degree of voluntary evacuation is certain to take place and we believe that all cities should have in hand plans to assist in controlling those movements. A corollary, of course, is the planning of suitable reception preparations for those who would need them following their evacuation from their homes.

The other consideration, as I mentioned, is the provision of shelter. A distinction must be made between shelter against the blast and fire effects of nuclear weapons and shelter designed to protect against radioactive fallout. The former type of shelter has much significance to residents of larger cities which might be the object of direct attack. For the majority of the Canadian people, however, protection against fall-out is much more significant and necessary, since it is the peril which is most likely to affect them. Even in the larger cities, if they are spared direct attack so that blast effects do not arise, fall-out shelters are of importance.

The government has given attention to many of the problems that arise with respect to fall-out. Target cities in arranging their survival plans must give and are giving attention to the positive steps they can take in the direction of both evacuation and shelter, and these plans will vary according to the different circumstances in existence from city to city.

The problem of appropriate types of shelter for Canadians in the varying circumstances is a complex one. Some live in private homes; others live in apartments, and there are considerable numbers in institutions of various kinds. It is felt that in addition to the information concerning shelters which offer a degree of protection and shelters suitable for occupancy for up to 14 days, consideration should be given to adaptations which would provide the same degree of protection at less cost. We should also suggest improvised types of protection suitable for shorter use, and makeshift arrangements where the protection offered is admittedly lower than might be considered reasonable but which will nevertheless give a degree of protection for short periods at least.

In this field of shelters, tenders have been called for construction at the Canadian civil defence college at Arnprior of a variety of prototype shelters. Some of these are designed for single families. Others will take

groups of families or other persons totalling as many as 30 occupants. Some will be blast resistant and some are designed to protect against fall-out only. These prototypes will serve for instruction and display, and will make possible investigation of living conditions in them, and, of course, they will be available for use in an emergency.

In addition to shelters in homes and other places of residence, it has been recognized that many larger buildings offer a good deal of potential fall-out protection. With modest preparations possibly involving relatively small costs, fall-out protection can be secured in such buildings for countless thousands of people. With a view to ascertaining which buildings have such possibilities and what their capacity may be, the government in the spring of 1961 authorized suitable surveys. The Department of Public Works proceeded with the work and has completed surveys of all federal buildings with a view to determining the amount of fall-out protection in them.

Members may be interested to learn that new techniques have been developed which enable the Department of Public Works to make these surveys quickly. I refer to the use of special cameras to determine the nature and character of the construction of buildings and the use of electronic computers to speed the securing of early results. This latter procedure came about through cooperation given by the Ontario department of highways, to whom the thanks of the government are extended. This is the type of survey now to be initiated in the United States. I understand that the Canadian methods have been reviewed favourably there and may be adapted for use in the survey recently announced in that country.

Some 4,820 buildings in Canada have been checked, and the Department of Public Works is now engaged in determining those that have adequate fall-out protection, those that can be improved to provide such protection, and others that cannot be thus improved due to the excessive costs involved. These surveys and their results will be available to the planners concerned shortly, and it will then be possible to determine how much of such accommodation could be made available to the public.

A new technical manual entitled ""An Engineer Looks at Fall-out Shelter"" has just been printed. It is designed for use by engineers and architects who will be responsible for carrying out surveys of existing fall-out protection in buildings and the possible incorporation of protective measures against fall-out in new buildings. These manuals are now being distributed and
should be invaluable to provinces and municipalities in undertaking their fall-out shelter surveys generally throughout the country.

In planning for the survival of our people, accurate public information is of vital importance, and during the past two years the government has authorized the publication of a series of pamphlets under the general name ""Blueprint for Survival"". These have included such booklets as ""Your Basement Fall-out Shelter"", ""Fall-out on the Farm"" and, more recently, ""Eleven Steps to Survival"". These pamphlets have been very much in demand, and as a result of the present international situation there has been a very large increase in requests in the last few weeks. More than a million copies of the publication ""Eleven Steps To Survival"" were printed up to July of this year, but it has become necessary to arrange for another large printing which is now in hand. This is indicative of the attitude and the feeling of Canadians as a whole. It is felt that publications which relate to the protection of the people under the possible perils of nuclear war deserve top priority in view of the widespread demand for full and up to the minute information.

Furthermore, there are other media of public information that will be used both nationally and locally, including the press, television and radio. The C.B.C. has been charged with the responsibility of developing an emergency radio broadcasting plan whereby adequate information can be made available to the public in the event of nuclear war even if normal broadcasting facilities are disrupted. C.B.C. studios are directly connected with army warning centres, and are capable of transmitting vital information to the public should the need arise.

In so far as a national exercise is concerned, the announcement was made recently that there will be another national exercise to test emergency plans. The last one was held in May, 1961, and served to inform the public of the plans that have been developed nationally, provincially and municipally. The forthcoming exercise, which I think will take place in early November, will enable the various warning arrangements to be used. It will bring home to individual Canadians and to the various levels of government their responsibilities and will enable an exploration of what can be done to meet the potential dangers. In short, the aim of such an exercise is to check the readiness of this country to meet the actual challenge of war if perchance that challenge should confront us.
The planning and preparations made by provinces and municipalities are important and cannot be overemphasized. I might refer to the financial assistance program of the

Supply-Privy Council federal government, which recognizes that planning of this sort is most significant as it gets nearer and nearer the people affected. That is why local planning is of such great importance. While the federal government can develop broad measures for Canada as a whole, and the provinces likewise within their respective boundaries, planning in detail can only be done at the local level. Hence the case for support and assistance in the costs that will be involved.

For some years the federal government has provided such financial support in respect of personnel and administration costs, supplies and equipment, training and all the other items that arise in the course of local planning. Included are communications equipment, construction costs for local emergency government headquarters, payment of fees for first aid training, purchase of protective clothing for volunteers and other emergency personnel, rescue equipment, vehicles, cost of local training exercises and publication of local survival plans including material on evacuation and shelter such as has been done by some of the larger cities. These costs are supported on approval to the extent of 75 per cent and when I say that these costs are supported I mean that they are supported from federal sources.

The federal government has provided $4,350,000 for this financial assistance program during the current fiscal year. To date projects totalling $3.5 million have been approved, of which the federal share exceeds $2.5 million, and a further volume of projects of an approximate value of $1.5 million is now being reviewed. It would appear that eventually more than $5 million in provincial and municipal projects will have been submitted this year, of which the federal government will pay some $3,700,000. This program of financial assistance has been generally admitted by the provinces to have been extremely helpful in provincial and local emergency planning.

In order that municipalities should have a degree of guidance in developing their local emergency plans, several significant steps have been taken by the federal government including the distribution of a publication ""A Survival Planning Guide for Municipalities"" and the provision of courses for mayors, reeves and councillors, as well as courses for municipal officials. This feature has been widely accepted by municipal officials.

I might point out that at the conference for mayors, reeves and wardens held in May at the Canadian civil defence college, some 69 attended. There were 64 present in October, 1960 at the Canadian civil defence college conference in respect to the provinces of Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Nova

Supply-Privy Council Scotia and Newfoundland. At the conference in Edmonton from November 4 to 7, 1960 for the three prairie provinces, British Columbia, Northwest Territories and the Yukon, 56 attended. A further course took place in Ontario from November 6 to 10, 1960 at the Canadian civil defence college, and 81 attended. There were further courses in March and June this year for the maritime area and also for the western area. In all, these courses were attended by some 414 mayors, reeves and wardens.

The foregoing measures are largely concerned with survival. There is a related and important aspect of emergency planning, and that is the continuity of government. This is being provided for in all NATO countries to assure that there shall be such continuity in the event that war comes. This continuity of government is being provided for, so far as it is possible to do so, for all levels of government. If people are to survive they will need leadership, not only national but provincial as well as municipal. The government has authorized the construction of emergency headquarters in each of the provinces to provide facilities for governmental operations in wartime.

Since permanent emergency headquarters will not be completed for some months, it has been found desirable to make available immediately interim emergency headquarters. These will have the necessary communications to ensure that operations can be carried on. Arrangements are in effect with regard to the provision of central facilities for the federal government. Similar facilities are now being provided in the provinces designed for use by a nucleus of federal public servants in each province and by various elements of the provincial government and its officials, and by the Canadian army. These regional headquarters are protected against radioactive fallout but are not provided with protection against blast effect. The headquarters are not in the so-called target areas.

This is an aspect to which reference is made from time to time. It is one of those things that are absolutely necessary. It was found to be necessary in the days of the last war when the probabilities of complete disruption of government by the destruction of capital cities was far less direct and fearsome than it is today.

With regard to other aspects of emergency measures, I should like to refer to the fields of transportation, meteorology and defence production, as well as health and hospitalization. In the field of transportation we have provided for the establishment of an emergency organization for the control of all types of transport, inland, coastal, water, civil aviation, and
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l

road. The Department of Transport is working in close relationship with all agencies involved. Qualified individuals have been and are being selected to serve on emergency transport organizations. Plans have been made for the control and administration in wartime of the whole civil and national telecommunications system to ensure the best possible use of communications that survive attack, and the identification of alternate routes where existing systems have been disrupted or destroyed.
Provision is being made for the continuation of meterological services across Canada, for they are vital from many points of view, not the least of which is the assessment of fall-out patterns.

The Department of Defence Production has planned the organization of a war supplies agency which will be responsible in wartime for the control, production and distribution of all supplies and the establishment of rationing and price controls if required. Individuals are being selected to serve on the war supplies agency in wartime, and studies are being made of the need for the stockpiling in peacetime of certain supplies to be located so as to be readily available for use by the population. The department has already achieved a certain capability to operate such an agency, both nationally and regionally, and has a well developed plan for a system of damage analysis in order to be able to calculate immediately what supplies remain after attack and from this to determine their best use.

Now I come to the question of health. The Department of National Health and Welfare is responsible for arranging and stockpiling essential medical items. This has now reached a cost of $9 million, with supplies placed at strategic points throughout the country. In many cases they have been redistributed and so located as to be available to provincial health services. Eventually this program will cost $18 million. Arrangements have been made to have available 200 emergency hospitals with total accommodation for 40,000 patients. These emergency hospitals can be set up on short notice, thereby adding greatly to the national capacity for taking care of the victims of a nuclear war. All nursing schools in Canada and six of the 12 medical schools have introduced into their curricula a study of emergency nursing and health procedure. Through the co-operation of the St. John's Ambulance and Red Cross, tens of thousands of men and women have been trained in first aid and home nursing procedures. It has been estimated that some 50 per cent of all hospitals in Canada now have disaster plans.

These are examples of the work of particular departments and agencies. Others are doing comparable work. A case in point is the planning by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police which will help support the efforts of the various attorneys general in maintaining law and order.

With a view to providing the necessary authority for control of all these areas of emergency action, special orders and regulations will have to be available for use in wartime. The federal departments concerned have already submitted proposals for the orders, and these are now being assessed with a view to assuring their adequacy and also to prevent duplication.
There are additional measures in a number of fields that are being studied, such as the following:

column2: The authorization for the emergency measures organization, through the C.B.C. and otherwise to arrange appropriate notices to draw public attention to shelter and other survival measures such as those set forth in the pamphlet ""Eleven Steps to Survival"".

Determination of the costs that will be involved in bringing selected federal buildings up to at least minimum standards of protection against fall-out and in providing essential facilities and supplies for survival of occupants under fall-out conditions.

Consideration of measures giving priority to target areas, which in the main include our larger cities, for increasing fall-out protection for those dwelling in private houses or apartment houses by making it possible for people to make use of government, privately owned, commercial and industrial buildings.

Arrangements for an early conference of federal and provincial ministers in the civil emergency planning field to review planning programs, training programs, financial aid measures and related matters.

Development by EMO of a pattern of decentralized units of emergency government on a zonal basis, each of these zones being smaller than regions, in order to provide the necessary backup to emergency arrangements for regional government and to ensure that survival programs are understood by the people concerned.

Consideration of measures to ensure the training of the great numbers of civilians required in rescue and radiation monitoring to be undertaken by federal, provincial and local authorities, this planning being additional to the army's current program in these fields.

column1: I should stress that most of the items of planning to which I have made reference have been under way for some time but the present international situation has tended to emphasize their importance. Looking back

Supply-Privy Council to what has taken place since 1959, may I say this. The basic arrangement then made, assigning the main civil defence responsibilities to four departments of government, has worked out very well. As I said a moment ago, the arrangement announced within the last few weeks by President Kennedy with respect to civil emergency planning parallels in many respects the arrangement which we have brought into effect. The assignments now given to the secretary of defence in the United States in respect of survival planning are very much similar to those carried out here by the Department of National Defence in the fields of warning, radiological monitoring, emergency communications and damage assessment.

There is a significant difference in the responsibility for the development of the shelter program, which is placed in the privy council office through the emergency measures organization. The current stress given to shelter in the United States, particularly with respect to the use of surveys to determine the protective capacity of existing buildings, is similar to the work we have been doing throughout the year 1961.

The creation of the office of emergency planning in the United States, which will be charged in the main with the co-ordination of all civilian wartime planning and with the responsibility of developing useful measures for the continuity of government, has brought into existence an agency comparable to the emergency measures organization which we have here.

I think these points are worthy of emphasis, for they indicate that Canadian planning, while it was focused on Canada and the specific needs of the Canadian people, is not unrelated to planning in the United States and, I might add as well, among our NATO allies generally.

This, Mr. Chairman, is not the kind of report one would relish bringing before the house. It is, however, necessary. We realize that in our country and in the free world there hangs over us from day to day the cloud of successive test explosions by the U.S.S.R., threatening in their import and I only hope not prospective of their use in the days ahead. I know there are some who say, ""Why do anything about it?"" These are measures designed as insurance to the highest degree possible for the survival of Canadians. I pray that they will never be used.

When I read some of the headlines I think it must be emphasized and re-emphasized that scaring people is not the course that democracies follow. Democracies, however, are sometimes slow to realize the danger, namely that the challenges of communism which
Supply-Privy Council

know no restraint but power, are being increased daily. The devotion of this government is to peace. The continued advocacy of disarmament has had that one purpose in mind. However, when you arrive at a point where everything you endeavour to do in order to bring about disarmament is met by the stone wall of formidable indifference coupled with continuing threats, the people in the free world must realize that every action a government can take for survival must be taken.

Peace is our aim. Peace is our dedication. Peace is the purpose for which the hours of government are taken. But at the same time we would be remiss if we did not do everything we can to preserve and maintain our country against the dread contingency that has been made more frightening by the repeated statements, each often more threatening than the last, that have characterized Mr. Khrushchev and his international revelations and plans during the last few months.

I do not say that what has been done is perfect. No plan that can be made will ever achieve the measure of perfection that all of us have in mind. Last evening I was reading Lord Hankey's book, which is in two volumes, on the days of war. He was the clerk of the British cabinet. After all, clerks of the cabinet are closer to international and national events than even the cabinet ministers themselves, for they have all the departments within their knowledge. He points out the number of trials that turned out to be errors. All the same, advances were made each time.

We are in a field that has never been seriously considered as a necessary one in the past. We are in a field of danger that has developed nationally and internationally. It has developed in increasing measure since 1948. I think we owe the thanks of the house and the country to those who are devoting themselves to this administration, to the voluntary workers, to those who are in charge of the organization, to Mr. Curry and those associated with him. After all, in so far as voluntary workers are concerned, they are giving their services, often thanklessly in the public mind, in their individual contributions to the survival of us all. Such service is of the highest order of good citizenship.
I have taken longer than I intended, but I ought to place before the committee in some detail the action that is being taken and some conception of the additional steps that we have in hand.

,Progressive Conservative,,John George Diefenbaker,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089&Language=E&Section=ALL
2140535,ca.proc.d.1961-09-13.30.3,1961-09-13,6ffdccf5-fe20-4be5-b99d-1593863458ac,ca.m.1985,Mr. Hellyer:,,PRIVY COUNCIL,,,Mr. Chairman, I am sure the committee has been indeed interested in the statement by the Prime Minister this morning. It was- a comprehensive statement in

many ways. It covered a great deal of territory. It also reflected an awakening of the government's interest in the subject of civil survival. It was delivered in a very serious tone. One cannot help but wonder whether that tone is reflected in the action being contemplated by the government.

It is interesting to note that another exercise will be held in November to test the adequacy of measures taken so far. We hope there will be a considerable improvement shown from the last exercise. We are sure this will be so. However, we still suspect that it will show up a considerable number of very fundamental gaps, and we feel these have to be discussed in greater detail. In considering this subject one must look at a fundamental question, is passive defence worth while? This depends on the kind of world in which we and our children will have to live.

It is a fact, as the Prime Minister indicated, that the United States and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics have great stockpiles of nuclear and thermonuclear weapons. It is also a fact that they are continuing the production and development of these weapons. Much time and effort has been spent attempting to negotiate a disarmament agreement, so far without success. This is a matter of profound regret to all of us. At the same time we must face the facts as they exist. If we must live under an umbrella of thermonuclear terror for a prolonged period, it may be advisable to take such effective steps as are open to us. As Rogers Cannell said:

A non-military defence program is very much more than a passive aspect of preparation for allout war. An extensive, well planned, thoroughly co-ordinated civil defence program is one of the best, most positive steps we can take to avoid war or blackmail threats of war.

The Russians know that we have as yet no real protection for our population. Knowing this, they are in a much stronger position to attempt atomic blackmail. The threat of an attack which would kill a large proportion of our population cannot be taken lightly.

Also, the Soviet know that we have no defence now. A dozen Bomarc squadrons and a dozen squadrons of Voodoos would not begin to provide us with any protection. As a matter of fact the fall-out from these so-called defensive weapons alone, if they are equipped with nuclear warheads, would be sufficient to wreak tremendous havoc amongst our civilian population. No, Mr. Chairman, we have no protection from these devices; we are as exposed as babes in the wood.
The true value of any defence program lies in its contribution to national objectives. If total war should come, and like the Prime Minister we pray that it will not, the survival

of the people-and they are the nation- would be a primary objective. It is virtually certain that at the present time and in the foreseeable future the most effective measures for national survival in the event of war are those which contribute most to the survival of the people. These same measures act as a considerable deterrent to those who would contemplate the launching of a total war.

The Russians themselves appreciate this position. They have already taken steps far in advance of ours, and most of the adult population has received extensive instruction in civil defence measures emphasizing radiological protection.

,Liberal,,Paul Theodore Hellyer,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=6ffdccf5-fe20-4be5-b99d-1593863458ac&Language=E&Section=ALL

,Progressive Conservative,,John George Diefenbaker,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089&Language=E&Section=ALL
2140537,ca.proc.d.1961-09-13.30.5,1961-09-13,6ffdccf5-fe20-4be5-b99d-1593863458ac,ca.m.1985,Mr. Hellyer:,,PRIVY COUNCIL,,,My authority for that statement is the Stanford Institute research program. The Russians, aware of the facts, train their population in such activities as decontamination, shelter improvisation and atomic, biological and chemical warfare protection. Our government, too, is in possession of the facts, but so far does not seem to take the subject as seriously as one might expect, if the information available to the civilian population is true.

I have often said that it is important, in considering a large problem, to first admit that it exists and then to gauge its magnitude. Once this has been done it is possible to take action on the required scale. If the job is worth doing it is worth doing well. It is useless for some people to have shelters, for example, and others not. In this case chaos would result, if war were launched. As someone said the other day, ""What sort of a problem would there be if the sirens sounded; if one person in a neighbourhood had a shelter and if women and children from other homes in the neighbourhood began to congregate there for protection?"" On what basis would the selection be made? What tests it would impose on human behaviour.

It is a question of all or nothing. If the job is to be an all-out job, it can only be done if the government provides the leadership, and in particular if it provides the financial assistance necessary to do the job. The magnitude is too great for individual initiative. Strong leadership is required, and strong leadership has not yet been forthcoming. The Prime Minister himself said this morning, ""If people are to survive, they need leadership"". We agree with that. We are glad to see this new interest.

As the Prime Minister indicated, at least by inference, it would not even be sufficient to have a shelter in every home. The requirement would depend on the time of day at which the attack took place. If it occurred

Supply-Privy Council during the day, for example, many children would be at school. It would be necessary to have effective fall-out shelters in schools and other public buildings. The Prime Minister has indicated that surveys are going to be undertaken to determine the adaptability of public buildings for fall-out shelters. The thing that would concern many people in a casual reading of the right hon. gentleman's statement would be the number of surveys which are now to be undertaken. One would wonder why some of them had not been undertaken sooner if the threat is as grave as was reflected in the Prime Minister's tone this morning.

The Prime Minister referred to evacuation. Certainly to have evacuation, warning would be required. Undoubtedly there might be some cases when evacuation would be necessary in the cold war. In times of extreme crisis or if we were under the threat of atomic blackmail, if adequate facilities were available for partial evacuation of our great cities it would add something to the credibility of the deterrent. But this is no substitute for urban residential shelters.

Then, too, the warning systems must be realistic, and as yet they are not. The sirens themselves are practically useless and often do not work. The signals are sometimes not understood. Sometimes they cannot be heard in all areas, and certainly not inside buildings with the windows closed. They cannot be heard when the weather is inclement, when there are storms, and they certainly could not be heard, in most cases, by sleepers at night. If the system is going to be of any use at all and if it is to effectively fulfil its function it has to be properly arranged. There is no question but that an effective warning system would require an individual type of warning, some device within every home and building which could be instantaneously activated either by telephone or by radio in the event of attack. The period of warning has become so short that no other means of communication would be adequate. Some automatic device would have to be developed which would be capable of coping with the situation.

In addition to the shelters and an adequate warning system, many other measures are required. The Prime Minister outlined a number of them in his statement this morning. These include facilities for the storage of food and materials, the provision of medical supplies and other necessities of life, facilities for re-entry and for rehabilitation. All these things must be attended to. It is obvious that to do the job properly even on a minimum scale is a major and expensive project. Any guess as to the probable cost without benefit

column2: HOUSE OF

column1: Supply-Privy Council of a thorough study would be highly speculative. It is obvious, however, that an expenditure of $3 billion or $4 billion would be required in as many years if shelter protection and warning systems were to be installed on a universal basis for our population.

It is the responsibility of the government to say whether or not the job is worth doing. The government is presumably in possession of all the facts; indeed, it sometimes gives the impression that it is endowed with prescience. If the job is essential we should be told and advised of the consequences. If the government does not think the task is worth undertaking it should say so and give the reasons, explaining at the same time why it is spending money on partial and inadequate measures.

What has the government done so far? In fact, very little, and in reverse order. It is true that it has set up an emergency measures organization. It is also true, as the Prime Minister reminded us this morning, that it has divided the responsibility among four and perhaps more departments. There are those who think this authority is too divided, that it is unworkable, because it lacks a straight line command.

I join the Prime Minister in his tribute to the individuals who are members of the emergency measures organization and others engaged in this work. They are doing the very best they can under extremely difficult circumstances. They are dedicated, competent individuals, and we wish them every success in what they are undertaking. But the real problem is the lack of leadership on the part of the government. This case has been put many times, once by the Globe and Mail in an editorial on Thursday, May 18, 1961. The article is entitled ""Survival Without Defence"" and reads in part as follows:
The core of the difficulty in evolving a comprehensive civil defence policy is the lack of a clear defence policy, which in turn would have to stem from a well-defined foreign policy.

In the opinion of some of us at least we still do not have a clearly defined defence and foreign policy. The government has, of course, built a shelter for itself. This is fine. The Prime Minister mentioned the necessity for the continuity of government. We hope he is not preoccupied with the continuity of the present government.

,Progressive Conservative,,John George Diefenbaker,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089&Language=E&Section=ALL
2140539,ca.proc.d.1961-09-13.30.7,1961-09-13,6ffdccf5-fe20-4be5-b99d-1593863458ac,ca.m.1985,Mr. Hellyer:,,PRIVY COUNCIL,,,I think the Prime Minister spends a great deal of time worrying about it. The government has purchased very little equipment. The government is now talking about prototype shelters. I must say I was surprised to hear that reference in the Prime

Minister's statement. I would have thought the prototypes would have been undertaken many months ago. Particularly I would have thought the prototypes would have been completed before pamphlets were prepared and distributed to the public indicating methods of construction.

In addition to those things mentioned by the Prime Minister this morning, most of which in substance are in the planning and survey stages, the government has mentioned the training of 100,000 additional troops for civil survival. This, on the face of it, sounds like a very fine idea. We certainly need more trained people to assist in the event of a national calamity. According to the figures given to the committee yesterday by the Minister of National Defence, the cost of the training of these individuals will be approximately $5 million per month for pay and allowances alone. On the basis of the total figure he gave us it is obvious there is no provision whatsoever for equipment. We are going to have a broomstick army. I can just see them now, the 100,000 men out with their brooms sweeping up the radioactive debris. Of course I forgot one thing. They will all be dead; they will, that is, unless an adequate shelter and warning system has been established in the meantime. The whole program has been backwards. It is useless to have a training scheme without the essential requirements of shelters, warning systems and a stockpile of supplies, etc.
It would be difficult to establish priorities, but certainly a proper priority would be to build the shelters, to install adequate warning systems and to undertake the training simultaneously.

So far we have been shadow boxing; so far the whole talk about civil survival has had an air of unreality. The people of Canada have a right to be told, and on behalf of the official opposition we demand that they be told, whether the government really takes this problem seriously or whether it does not; whether the government feels that we must have an adequate shelter and warning system or whether it does not. If the answer is positive, then there should be a positive program for effecting it. If the answer is negative, then there should be positive reasons given why they are not required. This is the responsibility of the government. This is what the people expect of their government.

This morning the Prime Minister said that the democracies are sometimes slow to realize the danger. I think that statement can be underlined. The question the Canadian people ask is whether this government has been slow to understand the danger. I hope that before the debate is ended someone will again

intervene on behalf of the government and tell the committee in clear and unequivocal terms whether the government is going to make the program work, whether it is worth working, or whether we are just going to continue, as we have in the past, to dabble with it.

,Liberal,,Paul Theodore Hellyer,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=6ffdccf5-fe20-4be5-b99d-1593863458ac&Language=E&Section=ALL
2140540,ca.proc.d.1961-09-13.30.8,1961-09-13,57dd42c2-427c-4252-9a45-f0c416cc0e1b,ca.m.5944,Mr. Pitman:,,PRIVY COUNCIL,,,Mr. Chairman, I am sure all hon. members were impressed with the seriousness of the situation as described by the Prime Minister this morning. I am sure also we were impressed with his frankness in indicating that this plan could not achieve perfection because we do not know exactly what kind of attack it will be, what the extent of it will be, or even the kind of weapons which will be used. Indeed, that is an understatement. We cannot achieve perfection, but surely we can give the Canadian people some sense of urgency, some sense of purpose and some sense of direction, something which has been entirely lacking over the past ten years.

This morning the premier of Ontario was quoted as saying, ""For the first time we have order out of chaos because for once the army has been brought into this whole matter."" This statement is made ten years after we have been threatened with thermonuclear war. The premier of Ontario called the efforts chaos. Evidently the only way a democratic nation can get out of chaos is by calling in the army. I think this is something which we as parliamentarians should be rather sober about. Indeed, I think the measures which were put forward this morning could have a good effect, but only if it is completely proven to the people of Canada that this government is serious about what is going on.

I thought the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Defence made a very good point yesterday when he said that we cannot put our heads in the sand. We cannot assume that because thermonuclear war will be so terrible, so horrible, therefore no human being would bring it about. We cannot be so completely devoid of recognition of human madness as to believe that war could not come. He is quite right. All of us in this house have been disgusted, have been angry and supremely disappointed over what the Soviet union has done in the past two weeks. Perhaps if some of us have not belabored Mr. Khrushchev as thoroughly as others-and this includes all parties-it may be because some of us have felt that there is no great advantage in belaboring Mr. Khrushchev.

There is a second way in which we can put our heads in the sand, and that is by failing to recognize the extent of the next war and the kind of attack which will be made. It is the feeling of many, I am sure, that our defence policies and our emergency measures policies are based on some kind of limited nuclear

Supply-Privy Council war. We have been told by people who should know that the U.S.S.R. has hundreds of bombers, and our emergency measures organizations are based on the assumption that only a few, maybe ten to 20, will get through.

This is an assumption for which I can find no strategic basis. We know the U.S.S.R. has missiles well on the way to development. We know they are capable of being fired now, yet our defence policies and our emergency measures organization policies are based on the belief that only one or two or three or four missiles will be fired in the first few hours. This seems unbelievable. We know that the Russians have a number of submarines. Some of them may be equipped with nuclear weaponry; yet we assume that only a very few will reach our shores, and only a few shots will be fired. I think this is the reason the people of Canada are so completely immune to the pleadings of the emergency measures organization people throughout the entire country. This feeling is found everywhere. People just cannot get very interested.

The Prime Minister mentioned the pamphlet which was sent out showing how to build a fall-out and blast shelter for $500. In Peterborough last March we tried to find out how many shelters were in the city. We could not find one shelter that had been erected. There had not been a building permit taken out for one shelter. This shows the extent to which the people of Canada are completely oblivious to the danger. They are basing their belief on the hope that there will be no war, or that it will be so complete that there is simply nothing that can be done about it, largely because of the attitude of the government which is based on the assumption that the kind of war which will take place is a limited nuclear war. Yesterday I sat in this chamber and was shocked by the remarks of the Associate Minister of National Defence when he said, as reported at page 8241 of Hansard:

If the worst should come, and If we have to fight again, I do not hesitate to say that we shall once again win the battles of tomorrow just as we won the battles of yesteryear, and this for many reasons. The main reason is that we have right on our side and that right in the days of tomorrow will triumph as it has always triumphed in former years.

We shall win the war of tomorrow. Is this the kind of war it will be? I wish the minister had stated that he meant a limited war. I can only assume he does not see the possibility of an all-out nuclear war in the future. Surely hon. members are convinced that no one will win the wars of the future, and any attempt to talk about winning thermonuclear wars is a deception.

column2: HOUSE OF

column1: Supply-Privy Council

This is what worries me most, the tact that the Associate Minister of National Defence, who has the information in regard to the kind of defence we are building, should be talking about a limited war. If he is sure that Russia has only a few missiles capable of reaching United States and Canadian shores, if he is sure that she has only a few submarines, then he should tell the people of Canada and not talk about winning wars of this kind. He should tell the people that they have nothing to worry about other than a limited war, for which the defence which we have and the emergency measures organization we are preparing will be sufficient. But that is not being done. We have no information whatsoever that this government believes it will be that kind of nuclear war.

I turn now particularly to the emergency measures organization. I do not intend to go into the background, the history of confusion, lack of purpose, lack of material resources and divided authority which makes Mr. Frost's comment about chaos very descriptive. If there is any government which should be concerned about taking the lead in this matter of national survival, it should be the federal government. As I have said, I was much impressed this morning, and I hope we are at the beginning of a new era. I hope we have turned the corner, and that the national government is going to do something about national survival.

I speak as a representative of a community which is not crying or whining for help. It has done as much as it is humanly possible to do to deal with the matter of an emergency measures organization. I have been to other communities where it is nothing more than an office held by some person who has pretty well given up trying to get co-operation. We have a mayor who has taken the lead as the head of the organization. I was shocked when I saw in the newspapers the remark of the mayor of Ottawa, who asked ""Shall we get out or shall we get under""? If she does not know it is certainly a terrible situation, because I understand that the federal government expects the mayors of the various municipalities to take the lead in this matter and to be aware of what is going on and what is being planned.

In the community that I represent the authorities have organized in every direction, including the police and fire departments and the Red Cross disaster service. It has been determined what the restaurants and cafeterias can do. It has been determined what Canada Packers, Quaker Oats and other industries can do. They have even brought the ham radio operators into the picture. Every effort has been made to determine exactly
what the community can do in terms of a national disaster. What the authorities are looking for is some direction from the top.

Last January an exercise was held in many parts of Canada, when the siren systems were tested. In my community 100 people were listening for them, and a very small percentage even heard them. The survival operation came and went with very few people even knowing that it had taken place. Some of us feel that the sirens are inadequate. Some even say that they are useless, that the pitch is too high and that they are completely unsuitable having in mind the conditions we have in this country. I would hope that serious reconsideration would be given in the very near future to the type of sirens being used. As soon as the exercise was over a letter was written indicating that the people of the area could not even be warned if a national disaster took place. Yet today nothing has been done; we still have the same five sirens.

The Minister of National Defence gave us to understand that a new test is going to be made with the idea of trying to fill the gaps that were indicated in the previous test, but so far nothing has been done. The Prime Minister talks about the gaps shown in exercise Tocsin. Let us get rid of the gaps that existed even before that. I would say that the whole idea of individual shelters in the basements of homes has to be reviewed in terms of the kind of all-out nuclear war which a great many experts are predicting. The very fact that protection for the Canadian people is based wholly on whether a person has $500 to build a shelter is in my opinion a national shame. Having in mind the hundreds of thousands of unemployed last winter, and the fact that a great percentage of our farmers are not even making $2,000 a year, how can it be expected that these people are going to be able to pay $500 in a year to build a shelter? There is the additional fact that if you build a shelter you are then assessed more on the building containing the shelter than previously. In other words, you will pay for the shelter for the rest of your life.

,Progressive Conservative,,James Stanley Speakman,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=7618d8f0-a535-4385-a1f2-3c21d0f13382&Language=E&Section=ALL
2140542,ca.proc.d.1961-09-13.30.10,1961-09-13,57dd42c2-427c-4252-9a45-f0c416cc0e1b,ca.m.5944,Mr. Pitman:,,PRIVY COUNCIL,,,If I could be sure of being alive, but that is the whole point that needs reassessment in terms of the type of war being predicted. We need to reassess the whole basis of our thinking. We would not sell Salk vaccine at $10 a shot, and neither should we be selling national survival on the basis of $500 for shelters in the basements of our homes.
In the pamphlet ""Eleven Steps To Survival"" there is set forth step by step a method by

which we can survive. I am very concerned about information I have received to the effect that this publication is not entirely reliable. I have a letter here written by a gentleman in my area who is a Ph.D. in nuclear physics, who has worked on nuclear reactors for some nine or ten years and has even invented and patented instruments to detect radiation. He has studied this pamphlet and has reached some very interesting conclusions as to the validity of the bases on which it has been written. He has this to say in the letter, and I am pleased to place this on the record:

My main concern is with the advice EMO is giving on fall-out shelters. Take first your booklet ""Eleven Steps To Survival"". On page 10 under ""Know the Facts About Radioactive Fall-out"" it is implied that the fall-out comes from activation of ""earth, stones, buildings"" etc.; but the decay rate stated on page 12 is that for fission products from the fission of U-235. But regardless of this inconsistency, if the radioactivity were from the earth, the lifetime of that radioactivity would depend on the locale, and one could not make any such general statement as is made on page 12. On page 14 the pamphlet states that the shelter given in ""Blueprint For Survival No. 1"" will stop 99 per cent of the radiation. This is not true. Eight inches of solid concrete will only stop about 90 per cent of the radiation; the difference between 99 per cent and 90 per cent may sound trifling but it means that the occupant of the shelter receives ten times as much radiation in the 90 per cent case as in the 99 per cent case.
Do you wish to call it one o'clock, Mr. Chairman?

2140553,ca.proc.d.1961-09-13.31.3,1961-09-13,84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089,ca.m.3212,Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):,Prime Minister,PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRESIDENT OF ICELAND,,,Mr. Speaker, with the leave of the house I should like to refer to the presence in the gallery of the president of Iceland, Mr. Asgeir Asgeirsson, who is not unused to parliamentary institutions. He was, for a period of years, a member of the parliament of Iceland and occupied successive portfolios, finally that of prime minister. Throughout the years, he has made a great contribution to freedom and to the maintenance of good relations amongst the nations. This country and Iceland have had close relations going back for a thousand years. Indeed, it is not for me to become controversial, but it is recorded that the discoverer of Canada, Lief Erikson, was of Icelandic origin and came here 400 or 500 years before the recorded discovery. Throughout the intervening years there have been close ties between our nations.

Today, there are around 24,000 people of Icelandic origin in Canada, and they have two representatives in the House of Commons, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) and the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Stefanson), and in the other place Senator Thorvaldson. This is an
Distinguished Visitors

indication of the persuasive influence that the possession of a parliamentary form of government for ten centuries has had on the thinking and the lives of those either born in or descended from that country.

During the days of war, Canadian troops were stationed in Iceland in the years 1940 and 1941. Later on, there was a Royal Canadian naval base at Iceland which made it possible to bring about, at an earlier date, victory in the battle of the Atlantic. Since the war Iceland has been one of those countries which has given itself to freedom. It is a member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and its position, so strategically placed, has made it an important bastion in the north Atlantic community.

I am sure I speak for all hon. members in the house in extending to him a warm welcome, to his wife and, if I may join therewith the foreign minister, Mr. Gudmundsson and Mrs. Gudmundsson, as well as other members of their party. I hope that their stay in Canada will be an enjoyable one and that in the years ahead, as in the past, we shall walk together in freedom.

,Progressive Conservative,,John George Diefenbaker,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089&Language=E&Section=ALL
2140554,ca.proc.d.1961-09-13.31.4,1961-09-13,51c861ef-0f17-4a79-8d9b-0854fb3ef33f,ca.m.6889,Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):,Leader of the Official Opposition,PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRESIDENT OF ICELAND,,,Mr. Speaker, it is with the greatest appreciation and pleasure that I associate the Liberal party with the welcome the Prime Minister has just extended to the president of Iceland, his wife and to the members of his party. I do so, Mr. Speaker, with all the greater pleasure because I have, myself, had the privilege of visiting Iceland twice and have been the beneficiary of the legendary hospitality of the friendly people of that island.

The president is the representative of a people who, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Dief-enbaker) has said, have deep and close links with our own country. It is a country which has sent many of its men and women to Canada who, with their descendants, have enriched every aspect of Canadian life, including the arts, the sciences, law and the public service. As we have just been reminded by the Prime Minister, there are two members of our own house who are of Icelandic descent. At a time when there are in the world those who are trying to gain respect by brute force and braggadocio, it is a refreshing privilege to welcome to this house and to our country the distinguished leader of a people who, a thousand years and more ago, had learned how to govern themselves peacefully through free parliamentary institutions and who, ever since then, have earned the respect of all peoples not by their power but by their civilized decency and their passionate devotion to liberty under law.

2140555,ca.proc.d.1961-09-13.31.5,1961-09-13,b815a117-7953-4900-b152-afc56dfc44a1,ca.m.5560,Mr. H. W. Herridge (Kootenay West):,,PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF PRESIDENT OF ICELAND,,,Mr. Speaker, on behalf of this group I associate our members with the best wishes that have been expressed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Pearson) to the president of Iceland and his colleagues who are present in the house today.

Iceland has been referred to as the grandmother of parliaments, having been in existence exactly 1,031 years this year, I believe. But through the reading of history and the developments that have taken place, I think it would be more correct to say that Iceland was the great aunty of parliaments. Incidentally, just a little while ago I was informed that the Icelanders formed the first republic in the British commonwealth of nations. In the northwest territories that was later incorporated in the province of Manitoba I am informed that an Icelandic republic was formed but it was later incorporated in the confederation of Canada without any difficulties whatever.

I believe our opinion of people is often related to our personal relations in addition to our reading and our attempt to understand other people. I am happy to say this, if you will pardon a personal reference, Mr. Speaker. Our family landed in Manitoba in the early days of this century, hoping to get started on a cattle farm. My father, who was rather green as far as Canadian ways were concerned, built a shack at a point where Cathedral avenue in Winnipeg bisects the railway that runs to Winnipeg Beach. It was a single board shack made out of shiplap. During the winter the temperature fell to 57 degrees below zero. Had it not been for the kindliness of an Icelandic dairyman-I think his name was Thorgeson-who lived somewhere close to us, we would all have been frozen to death that winter. We therefore have that memory for which to give them credit. Perhaps some hon. members on the government side wish we had frozen to death. We think of the great kindness of these people the first time we had ever been associated with people of Icelandic stock, having regard to the things they did for us. They were extremely practical compared to our impractical approach to Canadian life at that time. 2140559,ca.proc.d.1961-09-13.32.3,1961-09-13,b815a117-7953-4900-b152-afc56dfc44a1,ca.m.5560,Mr. Herridge:,,DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE,,,Mr. Chairman, I wish to take the opportunity provided on this vote to place before the committee certain criticisms that the party to which I belong feels should be made with respect to NATO. We recognize that the formation of NATO 12 years ago might well have been a wise move only because it might have been tempting to the Soviets at that time to fill the military vacuum that existed in western Europe. We were informed that NATO's original aim was to maintain the peace. Our fundamental criticism now stems from the fact that NATO appears to be becoming a vested interest of more importance in itself than NATO's original aim. In our opinion if NATO had consciously sought peace throughout the years it is most unlikely that we would have the so-called Berlin crisis today. From correspondence I have received within the last two or three days I am able to say that many intelligent Canadians are of the same opinion.

In our opinion until 1955 there was a real possibility that German reunification could have been bought for the price of German neutrality on a basis similar to Austria's. However, already in 1955, those who view history only in military terms, those who believe that foreign policy is merely a question of armed strength and who depend on that alone, were already on the ascendency in NATO. Rather than doing everything possible to bring about a peaceful settlement to the problems created at the conclusion of world war II, other steps were taken. In the opinion of the party for which I speak NATO aggravated those problems by decid-

Supply-National Defence ing on the rearmament of Germany. If anything could have been better designed to prevent the reunification of Germany and to aggravate the problem of Berlin, I do not know what it could have been.

2140576,ca.proc.d.1961-09-13.32.20,1961-09-13,b815a117-7953-4900-b152-afc56dfc44a1,ca.m.5560,Mr. Herridge:,,DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE,,,Mr. Chairman, this is conditional support given to NATO as a result of the convention decision of the New Democratic party. At the same time I am trying to bring to the attention of the house certain other features with respect to the administration of NATO that are causing serious and increasing concern, and that is why I mentioned the appointment of General Heusinger. The New Democratic party has accepted that Canada should remain in NATO for the present provided NATO does not become the vehicle for the further spread of nuclear weapons. The majority in the New Democratic party hope that on coming into power the New Democratic party government will be able to effect the basic changes in NATO's policies, strategy organization and attitudes that have in our opinion become essential. In our view the aim of western diplomacy should not be to perpetuate NATO but rather to strive to bring about those conditions that will make NATO obsolete. To achieve success in this endeavour is in our opinion to fake a long step forward to achieving peace.

When the second world war started, Mr. Chairman, the western aim was to prevent Germany attaining hegemony over eastern and central Europe, but at the end of the war the western aim had become to destroy Germany's power for generations, if not forever. I am speaking of her military power and not the power of her people to rise again and develop a great culture. The result was that the west allowed the Soviets to attain
that consolidation in eastern and central Europe which we had sought to deny to Germany.

In 1949 the aim of NATO was to maintain the peace. Now all we hear in NATO is the necessity of maintaining western unity. There is a difference in perspective and outlook there. History is repeating itself and it will continue to do so as long as we allow military thinking to dominate NATO and the minds of western statesmen.

What use was the winning of the last war when we so obviously lost the peace? What use will there be in maintaining western unity when we will all be united only in the grave if we go on as we are now?

Let us get back to the original aim of NATO-peace. Let us strive to bring the NATO powers to work for a settlement in Europe. Remaining in the position reached by our victorious armies 16 years ago is not a settlement. It is not even an armistice, for we are now engaged in an arms race with a former ally who, incidentally, lost some six million men in battle and uncounted millions owing to the savagery of the German armies that they were fighting.

Because of these considerations, Mr. Chairman, we object most strongly to the present so-called military build-up. In terms of the terrible power of the thousands of H-bombs that would be unleashed in the event of war breaking out, the sending of 2,000 additional troops by Canada to Europe is absurd. It is also provocative, for it shows not determination, not a desire to strive for the original aim of NATO which was peace, but rather a desire to strive by force of arms to maintain the status quo in Berlin. If the west was truly protecting the freedom of West Berliners, then our reaction could be understood. However, all our troop reinforcements really indicate, and apparently are intended to indicate, is the bareness of new concepts in the minds of the leaders of the west.

What makes our military gesture all the more farcical, all the more silly, from our point of view, is that we are not sending a single additional military unit to Europe but are simply making good the attrition or wastage of front line troops caused by the well known inclination of peacetime military forces, like other bureaucracies, to indulge in luxuries when no one is looking. We know that they have extra batmen, extra cooks, extra gardeners and extra people doing chores. What we are actually doing is replacing the loss of combat troops who are now performing other services. When our military forces went to Europe initially, they went as a full establishment at least, we were told that. If they are not at full war establishment now

Supply-National Defence the reasons can be found in the administrative headquarters commanded by a full colonel in Antwerp and in the officers clubs, leave centres and recreational facilities in which peacetime armies abound.

If the Minister of National Defence really thought the front line units should be brought up to strength, he had only to round up and send forward all the rear echelon types who have grown up around our army brigade group and our air division over the last ten years. Anyone with any experience in military affairs knows that this happens.
