It is extremely hard to imagine that a fire, in an area which is not heavily wooded, could move eight miles, as that fire did, in the course of a single day. However, that is what happened.

I think the facts of this situation are not nearly as well understood as they perhaps should be. For two successive summers there has been virtually no rain in Newfoundland and during last winter the ground froze before the snow came. The result was that when the snow melted there was a quick runoff and the ground was drier than anyone who had seen Newfoundland only before 1960 could have believed was possible in that province. I am not amazed that there were as many fires as there were. I am really amazed that there were not even more of them. I think it says a good deal for the care that was taken by the whole population that there were not more fires and that most of them were kept in as good control as they were kept. However, there is no question whatever that, without the rain that came on that particular week end, while the troops might have saved a few settlements they would not have been able to do anything more to stop the fires in the forest any more than were those people who had previously been fighting them. However, the two things-the arrival of the troops and the rain-happened fortunately to coincide, although there have since been outbreaks. It is really very sad but each time the rain comes and even in spite of heavy rain, the ground is dry again within half an hour because there is just no moisture in the soil, and the rain evaporates so rapidly.

However, to come back to the point about which I am really concerned, may I say this and I think there will be a good deal of surprise about this situation. I know that most people I have talked to were surprised to discover that although the federal government acted with the greatest possible promptitude when requested to do so on both occasions and everybody has the greatest possible gratitude for that fact I think there is a good deal of surprise not only in Newfoundland but on the mainland when people realize that this assistance is not a national service given in a national emergency but is something that has to be paid for. It is

Supply-National Defence true that not the whole of it has to be paid for, as was pointed out by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George in answer to a question this morning, but there is a considerable charge. I feel that the committee would wish to know what this charge is, what the basis of it is and what is behind it.

I think every sensible person recognizes the fact that the armed forces cannot be at the beck and call of every local authority or even every provincial government every time a house burns down and that there must be some reasonable safeguard against that sort of thing. However, we know that there have been other kinds of disaster in this country, even this year, in which the greatest possible generosity was shown by the federal authorities at the cost of the national treasury. The loss in this particular case-I refer to the case of the fires this year-in the province of Newfoundland is in some respects a loss that is going to go on as far ahead as the human mind can conceive because what has happened in part of that area-and happily only in part of it-is this. The situation is not just that the trees have burned. It is not just that the forest has burned. The situation is that the soil, or what there was of it, has also all burned. What is going to happen to a good deal of the cape Freels peninsula, is that when the winds come the ash will be blown away and there will be nothing left but bare rock. Then we will have to think in terms of geological time before anything will ever grow there again, except perhaps a little moss and maybe some blueberries. This is a really tragic loss of our forest resources.

Happily, in many other areas the fire raced through so fast that only the foliage on the trees was burned. The wood can be salvaged and the land is still there. But it is a tremendous blow to the province. I am not seeking in any way to be controversial or critical; I am merely seeking to get all the facts. I hope that when all the circumstances are taken into account, whatever the practice may have been in the past, the government will come to the conclusion that this was a matter of such national importance that it would not be appropriate in this particular case, in this particular circumstance, to follow the practices of the past. I hope the government will consider that whatever the armed forces may have done in Newfoundland should be regarded as a national contribution to that province in the face of a great disaster that is going to cost the province a great deal in its budget this year, taking into account the other measures it has taken to fight the fires. Unhappily-and this is the worst part of it- it has taken away the livelihood of a large number of our citizens.

2140619,ca.proc.d.1961-09-13.32.63,1961-09-13,546df72b-fbe3-4980-ad0f-abc7a4ceed2a,ca.m.876,Mr. Harkness:,Minister of National Defence,DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE,,,A very good summary of what transpired at that meeting was carried in the January 13 issue of the Halifax ""Herald"" in an article written by a newspaperman who was present to observe the situation at that meeting with respect to defence. The article reads:

Within the three days, the assembled delegates, or committees of them, proposed the country be taken out of the North American Air Defence Command (NORAD), then put it back in again and finally favored it being left half in and half out. And it was practically the same with the problem of what to do about nuclear weapons. One military commentator who was quoted yesterday by an hon. gentleman opposite had the following to say in connection with the position of the Liberal party with respect to defence. This is to be found in the February 1961 issue of the Canadian Commentator in an article by John Gellner:

This month's Liberal party rally has provided a dismaying example of what must happen if a military problem is resolved entirely on the basis of political considerations. The problem in question was that of Canadian participation in the North American Air Defence Command (NORAD). The resolution, as it was reported, suffers somewhat from confused terminology-it approves ""identification"" of suspected aerial intruders by Canadian fighter aircraft, but not ""interception"", although the former action is not possible without the latter. Still, it is quite clear what the stand is which the Liberals are taking in this matter: They want 90205-6-525J

Supply-National Defence to leave all arrangements as they are except that Canadian forces in NORAD would not actually shoot. In other words, we would warn the Americans that the enemy was coming, we would tell him who he is, we would fix and track him, but then we would virtuously withdraw and let the Americans do the killing. This is a solution worthy of Pontius Pilate, not of a Lester B. Pearson and his associates.

I think this is a very good summing up of the position taken on defence at the Liberal meeting and is one of the great reasons why everybody has been in doubt on it since. Gellner goes on in this way:
The policy which the Liberal party has adopted in this matter does not even make sense.
That is the situation. Until the Liberal party itself produces something that makes sense I really do not think we should spend too much time discussing its deficiencies.

The hon. member for Peterborough of course made a speech in favour of peace. Well, we are all in favour of peace and nobody will quarrel with him over his desire to attain peace; but I must say to him, in the language of a gentleman who is well remembered in this house, the Hon. Humphrey Mitchell, ""in a kindly way"", that I do not think he had very much to say really about defence. Therefore I have not very much that I can say about his contribution to it.

There is only one point really that I should touch on. He said we should have a mobile force capable of taking action in any part of the world under the United Nations. Well, of course, we have it. We have had it right along. We have been in the position for several years that whenever the United Nations made a request to us for a force we filled that request. The only way in which we can be in a position to meet any requests along this line that the United Nations may make is to have an army in being. We have got to have people trained in all arms, particularly people in the engineers, RCEME, signallers, and so forth. If you have a balanced army of that kind, in which you have all arms, when you are called upon to make a contribution to a force in NATO you are in a position to make it and make it immediately. This is the only way in which it can be done.

Up to date, every time the United Nations has called upon us to supply a force it has been a different type of force, and the only way we have met those demands, as I say, is by having a force of all arms, and having it well trained. Then when a demand is made on you you can meet it. We are in that position and have been in that position for some time past. This is a proposition which is stated very frequently as if it were something that did not exist and something that we should produce, namely a force for

Supply-National Defence the U.N. Well, as long as we have a standing army, as we have, then we can produce the force that the U.N. may require from us, within the limits of that army, of curse, at very short notice whenever we are asked, and up to date that is exactly what we have done.

The hon. member for Peterborough did not say much about NATO membership. The hon. member for Kootenay West went into it to some length. I would just like to say there is no doubt at all that the New Democratic party-is that the name of it?-is in a very equivocal position so far as NATO is concerned. The C.C.F. party, of course, condemned NATO. They said that we should get out of NATO and it should be done away with. They condemned NORAD. They said that we should reduce our armed forces very materially; that we should devote the money instead to foreign aid. In other words theirs was a pacifist and neutralist position, although they always denied that this was so, but in effect this is what it was. It called on Canada to get out of NATO, to get out of NORAD, but it was a definite position; it was one that you could understand, and if you accepted certain premises it was one for which I think you could argue. The hon. member for Kootenay West was a strong proponent of that position and he indicated in his speech today that he still believes in it, but he is in the unfortunate position of supporting a party that does not believe in it and therefore I sympathize with him.

The New Democratic party came about as a result of the union of the C.C.F. and the labour union people. The labour union congress, of course, takes a totally different view from the C.C.F. They believe in NATO. They say we should belong to NATO. As a matter of fact, I have here the two latest issues of the official labour magazine, the Journal of Canadian Labour Congress. Mr. Jodoin has an article in one and Mr. MacDonald has an article in the other. They both say that NATO must be supported; that we must remain in NATO; they condemn neutralism and so forth. I will not bother reading these various articles. Anybody can get these magazines; in fact I shall be glad to lend them to the hon. member for Kootenay West, if he has not read them, so that he may learn just what the attitude of the labour party is toward NATO.

2140623,ca.proc.d.1961-09-13.32.67,1961-09-13,546df72b-fbe3-4980-ad0f-abc7a4ceed2a,ca.m.876,Mr. Harkness:,Minister of National Defence,DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE,,,No. They accepted a nuclear strategy in 1954. They have made affirmations about it, which are matters of public record, on numerous occasions since. Various countries in NATO have entered into bilateral agreement with the United States and as far as having nuclear weapons on their soil is concerned, they have them available under the command of the NATO commander for use and so forth. In other words, NATO has been a nuclear power in effect for years and NATO adopted a nuclear strategy. Therefore, this proposition that if NATO as a whole adopts nuclear weapons, or any of the countries individually, that Canada should not belong to it, is contrary to the situation which exists. This has been the case right along and this resolution which was adopted by the New Democratic party is merely eyewash. It is merely a means by which the people there were deceived and the country generally; or otherwise the people who drafted this did not know anything about NATO and did not understand NATO. This matter is very clear. I hold in my hand the North Atlantic Treaty Organization handbook of 1959. It has in it various resolutions that have been passed in different years. Here is one, for example. It is the text of the declaration and communique of the December, 1957, ministerial meeting of heads of government. It states this, in connection with countering the Soviet threat, both nuclear and conventional:
To this end, NATO has decided to establish stocks of nuclear warheads, which will be readily available for the defence of the alliance in case of need.

In view of the present Soviet policies in the field of new weapons, the council has also decided that intermediate range ballistic missiles will have to be put at the disposal of the supreme allied commander Europe.
The deployment of these stocks of missiles and arrangements for their use will accordingly be

decided in conformity with NATO defence plans and in agreement with the states directly concerned. The NATO military authorities have been requested to submit to the council at an early date their recommendations on the introduction of these weapons in the common defence. The council in permanent session will consider the various questions involved.

As I say, NATO has had a definite nuclear strategy for all these years and therefore this is in complete contradiction of the resolution passed only two months ago, I believe, by the New Democratic party. According to the resolution passed by the New Democratic party, we should have been out of NATO several years ago. The thing is nonsense. It is just nonsense of the worst kind.

I have been surprised that this has not been pointed out long before now by some of the newspapermen who attended the convention, because it is a self-apparent fact that the resolution just does not make sense.

In addition to the official handbook of NATO which makes the position quite clear, it has also been made known in the newspapers on numerous occasions-I have some quotations I could give but I do not think I will take the time-that a number of NATO countries have made bilateral agreements to have nuclear weapons on their soil, which they now have, and to exercise joint control of such weapons with the United States. There are several countries of NATO in which that is the situation. Therefore when members of the New Democratic party and other people say that Canada should not be the first to join the nuclear club meaning the three countries who are actually producing nuclear weapons, the United States, Great Britain and France, they are not stating the situation correctly at all. Several countries have already, as these people refer to it, joined the nuclear club. Nuclear weapons have been placed on their soil and are there. I think certain matters along this line should be made clear because there seems to have been a great deal of confusion in the minds of many people as to what the actual situation is.

There was another point mentioned by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam in the external affairs debate which I think I should clear up because great confusion has been caused. He said that there were so many tons of t.n.t., ten tons or something like that, in the nuclear stockpiles of the United States and Russia for every man, woman and child in the world, and surely we did not need any more because this was enough to blow up the whole world. The whole point is that you might have enough nuclear power in a stockpile in a particular spot in Russia to blow up the whole world a hundred or a thousand times over but if they do not have the means
Supply-National Defence of delivering that nuclear power it does not do them any good. In fact, it can only serve as a potential danger to them.

In other words, the important thing in connection with nuclear weapons really is not the total number that you have some place in a stockpile but the means of delivery that you have for those nuclear weapons. As I pointed out in the speech I made and as I have pointed out on numerous occasions during the past several months, the Russians have not, as a lot of people are always attempting to show, an unlimited number of rockets and intercontinental ballistic missiles. In fact, they have a very limited number of intercontinental ballistic missiles capable of delivering nuclear weapons to this continent. Actually their chief means of delivery at the present time would still be by bomber and would have to be by bomber.

I mention this point particularly because I see letters and articles in the newspapers all the time. I recall one particularly in which it was said that a thousand of these nuclear weapons will be landed in Canada by intercontinental ballistic missiles. This is a complete impossibility. I am afraid that many of the people who are talking this way are doing so with the deliberate idea of trying to scare people and frighten them into adopting a pacifist or neutralist attitude. In other words, this is really a means of carrying to the Canadian people the terror tactics of Khrushchev. Khrushchev is talking about creating a 100-ton megaton bomb and dropping it on us. This is a terror tactic and we must recognize that it is a terror tactic. When he does this a lot of people in this country say, ""Well, you know how much damage was done by the bomb dropped on Hiroshima which was only one fifth of 1 per cent as large and if one such bomb were dropped on Ontario the whole of the province would be wiped out"".

A certain gentleman who writes letters to the newspapers has complained about the fact that he predicted such a bomb would be produced and that some of the papers had scoffed at him, and that I had scoffed at him. The important point in this connection is that the destructiveness of such a bomb does not increase directly in relation to its size. In fact, it is on the basis of the square of the cube root of the distance or something along that line. In any event, to put the matter in terms that people can understand I had our experts on these matters produce a little table for me. Let us take a 20 kiloton weapon. It has a certain power of destruction. The area of complete destruction is 1.1 square miles and the radius of complete damage is 2.2 square miles.
My arithmetic is not very good but let us take a weapon a million times larger. To make

Supply-National Defence it simpler, let us take a five megaton weapon and a 100 megaton weapon. With the five megaton weapon you have a radius of complete destruction of 3.9 miles while in the case of the 100 megaton weapon it is 10.5 miles. It is not 20 times as great; as a matter of fact, it is not quite three times as great. This point has to be kept in mind. The area of complete damage in the one case is 47 square miles and in the other case it is 346 square miles. The area of damage of all kinds, light damage and so on, is in the one case 610 square miles and in the other case 3,900 square miles. The area of dangerous fall-out in the case of the five megaton bomb is 2,500 square miles and in the case of the 100 megaton weapon it is 8,000 square miles.

I mention this because of the fact that the Khrushchev terror tactics of threatening to drop these 100 megaton weapons on people are being helped, I think, by a lot of people in this country who automatically take it for granted that if a one megaton bomb does so much damage a 100 megaton bomb will do 100 times as much. This is not the case and, as anybody who is familiar with explosives knows, the force of the explosion dissipates quite rapidly, with distance. I think we should know what the actual facts are. The people of Canada are entitled to know what the actual facts are in connection with these matters and those people who are trying to persuade them to accept something which is incorrect should themselves be exposed to the truth if they are not already aware of it.

The hon. member for Fort William spoke about the need for an armoury at Fort William. We are well aware of the need for armouries throughout Canada. There is a long list of places which need armouries and we would like to build them. However, armouries do no come very high on the priority list. There is only a certain amount of money available for defence and it is not possible for us to build all the armouries we would like to build. We have an armoury construction program under which we built a certain number of armouries, but nothing like the number that are being requested. This is not entirely satisfactory, but I think it will meet the need to some extent at any rate.

The hon. member for Kootenay West stated that he and his party were against sending any more troops to Europe, that this was just a waste of men, that no new units were being sent, and that the people being sent over were only replacing troops from the combat units that had been taken out for administrative duties to be cooks, batmen and goodness knows what, according to the story. This is completely incorrect. This is not the case at all. First of all may I say that two new units are being sent. An Honest John battery is going to be sent. I think it takes 235 men. A light helicopter reconnaissance unit is going to be sent. It takes some 75 men. The other 800 men are required

really because, contrary to what the hon. member for Trinity has said, the equipment of the brigade in Europe has been steadily built up and increased during recent years. The brigade was sent over there with one squadron of armour. It now has a full regiment of armour. One squadron of armour represents approximately 200 men. A full regiment at full strength represents approximately 800 men. That is a difference of 600 men right there. The brigade has been supplied with a great many other pieces of equipment since it went overseas, such as recoilless rifles and so on. It has been supplied with many more vehicles so that the whole brigade is mobile. They can all be put in the vehicles and moved at one time. That is why these extra men are required, not as cooks or batmen or to replace cooks or batmen. In other words the hon. member was speaking of what he knew not when he made that statement.

As far as the costs are concerned, may I say this. The costs which, on the normal basis, a province is expected to pay are not the pay and allowances. We charge nothing for that. But if there are any militiamen who are called out, then the province is expected to pay the extra pay and allowances for those militiamen. Then there are the transportation costs or in other words what it costs to bring the troops from the point at which they are located to where the fire is. Then there is the cost of equipment which is used up and lost, such as fire hose; or if there is a vehicle that is caught and burned in the fire and so on-any equipment which is used up or lost. Also it includes extra costs which may be incurred for lodgings, meals and things of that kind, whenever it is applicable. Generally it is not applicable. I have here a clipping from Life magazine, issue of August 25, 1961. It is entitled ""The Long Road Back for the Army"". I should like to read it for the benefit of the committee:
The conventional-war threat implicit in the Berlin situation poses some obvious questions about the U.S. army. The answers are disturbing.

Across the sand hills and pine woods of South Carolina the spendidly trained 101st and 82nd airborne divisions fought a rugged week-long battle that was billed as ""the most important land warfare exercise in 20 years"". It was a convincing show of strength, but the sad fact is these two divisions constitute two thirds of the combat-ready U.S.-based army. Most of their equipment is of world war II or Korean vintage, and much of it is wearing out. Not only the airborne divisions but the five first-line U.S. divisions in Europe are still using old tanks, and the quality of tanks has been the weak link in the U.S. arsenal. Only one battalion in the entire army is equipped with the new M-60 tank to match Russian T-54's which have been in operation since 1952. The Russian army, after two post-war equipment changes, has handed out to satellites and even neutralist Arabs newer equipment than the best-armed G.I. now carries.
This sorry situation came about largely because of the army's orphaned status during the eight-year era of the massive retaliation doctrine. After Korea

Supply-National Defence the army was cut back to less than 25 per cent of the total defence budget and barely managed to avoid obliteration by getting into the missile and rocket business. The army's Redstone has become a mainstay in the space race, but this kind of development tended to obscure the army's conventional role. ""After a while there wasn't any more fat to be chopped so they cut logistical bone and muscle and called it fat,"" says one colonel. ""Now the army is 60 per cent of what it looks like on paper."" The ground forces have another legitimate complaint: the air force has always placed too low a priority on the job of supplying planes and pilots that would turn the army into a swift and mobile world wide striking force.

Demoralized and unsure of its mission, slapped down repeatedly by congress and the defence department, the army's top leadership has grown fusty and defensive. By the time Kennedy stepped in and authorized 133,000 new men to beef up limited-warfare capability, the army's overlapping technical services and weakened logistical systems were so messed up that army brass wanted to assign most of the new manpower to noncombat functions. The administration, disillusioned with the brass, is still trying to find the handle for a more effective troop build-up as well as for basic reforms. Defence department civilians and the younger officer corps share the administration's sense of frustration. ""What we need,"" one of them says, ""is a guy who is smart, mad at the way things are, and a real S.O.B.""

The hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville referred to the situation in St. Jean, as well as in neighbouring areas, with respect to salaries which are paid by the Department of National Defence to employees on a part-time or hourly basis.
Among other things, the hon. member stated that, before 1957, the department's employees used to get annual increases.

That policy of paying hourly paid government employees salaries in keeping with the prevailing rates of the area for a similar work, has remained unchanged for years. The Department of National Defence makes sure that salaries paid to all hourly paid employees are reviewed at least once a year, and that increases are approved whenever they are warranted.

The hon. member added that since 1957 in some cases, and since 1958 in others, no salary increase had been granted. I am sorry to contradict him, but all the hourly-paid employees in the St. Jean area, except three, had a salary increase in 1958. In addition, other increases were approved in 1959 for almost all classes while other increases were approved in 1960 for certain classes of employees. Results of the preliminary study made by the department for the year 1961 on the rates paid in those areas are not yet available, unfortunately.

The hon. member mentioned that waitresses, assistant cooks, kitchen hands, truck drivers and others receive inadequate salaries that are too low to enable them to provide a decent living or even bare necessities for their families. The Department of Labour is responsible for the policies to be followed in the fixing of salary rates; in order to set these rates, we study the existing conditions in private enterprise.

The hon. member also mentioned that in the past, that is before 1957, employees who were not under the civil service could work overtime and earn higher salaries. There was no change made in that policy of paying

higher wages for overtime, but it has never been a practice, in the Department of National Defence, to provide on purpose overtime work as a means to increase the employees' salaries. On the contrary, they are asked to work overtime only when there are serious reasons for it. We do this in order to avoid additional expenses.

These last few years, the department and the R.C.A.F. have been particularly conscious of the fact that it is necessary to cut expenses whenever it is possible, while maintaining a high degree of efficiency.

The hon. member stated that, prior to 1957, the employees working on Saturdays or Sundays received higher pay, since they were paid at time and a half rates and sometimes at double time rates while today they are paid at straight time.

Mr. Chairman, I will answer by saying that hourly paid employees are entitled to a certain extra rate for the number of hours worked in addition to their normal week. Moreover, they are paid for the work done on days of rest, above and beyond their regular number of working hours.

However, it must be understood that because of the nature of the duties they have to perform, some employees work only on Saturday, Sunday or at night. Those are therefore considered as regular hours of work, not overtime.

I would be very happy to send the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis), a copy of the explanation given to me by the department and which should convince him that the Department of National Defence commits no injustice deliberately or otherwise towards its employees in the St. Jean district or elsewhere.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to comment briefly on certain remarks which were made to the committee this afternoon by the hon. member for Kootenay West. He referred to the fact it was rather inadvisable to permit German generals who have, at some time or other, served against our country, to occupy

I fully agree with the hon. member concerning the employment of well-known Nazis in positions of high importance. I am convinced that no friends of the Nazi party or well-known Nazis, and certainly no well-known war criminals, are employed in any capacity in NATO.

In so far as General Heusinger is concerned, I feel that it is necessary to mention that this distinguished officer was never at any time a member of the Nazi party or of the Nazi forces. A distinction must be made between the forces of the regular German army and the members of the Nazi party. General Heusinger was, in fact, a career officer in the Germany army. After the uprising of July 20, 1944, at which time there was an attempt on Hitler's life by a group of officers who believed the time had come to put an end to this madman's antics, General Heusinger was arrested and escaped from gaol just before he was sentenced to death by the Nazi party.

General Heusinger is a man who served his country with distinction. I believe we must realize that, in spite of the excesses of the Nazi party in Germany during the last war, there were nevertheless some patriotic Germans who felt that by serving in the army of their country they were serving their country just like so many Canadians, Americans and British soldiers felt they were serving their country by being in uniform. General Heusinger was never a Nazi. He was a man who was under sentence of death because he tried at one time to stop the evil effects of the Nazi doctrine upon the world. I felt that these remarks were necessary at this time.

2140694,ca.proc.d.1961-09-13.33.51,1961-09-13,dbc81dd3-47f7-4448-a205-ccbf43047e83,ca.m.8658,Mr. Martin (Essex East):,,19B1,,,What is clear, however, is that the government has not succinctly stated its policy. After all, the government was elected not only to formulate policy in all spheres of national and international activities, in so far as the latter apply to Canada, but also to see that these policies were given effect.

The government has not given us a clear statement with regard to the acquisition of nuclear weapons. I wish to say something about that at greater length than I can in the time at my disposal. I wish to indicate to the minister that I do propose, as others in this party have done, to call upon him to give now, before this house adjourns, a clear statement of the government's intention in this regard.

We do not wish to be confronted, with regard to this vital matter at this critical time in human history, with the device this government has employed on so many occasions. We were told, for instance, in the dying days prior to adjournment, that the government's policy with regard to amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act would be made known in due course.

The government stated in January in the speech from the throne that it was going to bring down amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. Then, the moment parliament adjourned we were confronted with a device which removes from the government any immediate, apparent responsibility. I refer to the appointment of a royal commission to go into something in connection with which the government said in January it was prepared to enunciate a policy.
Now we may be here another month. I have no doubt, from every indication now

apparent, that before we come back here in November or December the Minister of National Defence will announce a policy regarding the acquisition of nuclear weapons, and without parliament being given the opportunity of confronting the issue immediately and debating the question on its merits.

I believe that at a time when we are all seeking to appreciate the responsibilities of the government in this difficult period, it should take parliament into its confidence. The government should indicate what is in its mind.

,Liberal,,Paul Joseph James Martin,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=dbc81dd3-47f7-4448-a205-ccbf43047e83&Language=E&Section=ALL
2140695,ca.proc.d.1961-09-13.33.52,1961-09-13,intervention,,,,19B1,,,Hear, hear.

,,,Some hon. Members:,
2140696,ca.proc.d.1961-09-13.33.53,1961-09-13,dbc81dd3-47f7-4448-a205-ccbf43047e83,ca.m.8658,Mr. Martin (Essex East):,,19B1,,,The Minister of National Defence could rise in his place right now and say that Canada proposes to accept nuclear weapons without condition, or under certain conditions-in the custody of the United States, for instance, and under their control, but under arrangements that recognize the responsibility of the government of Canada in respect of matters pertaining to the welfare of this nation.

The minister can say that we propose to accept in Canada the agreement the United Kingdom has with regard to the acquisition of nuclear weapons in that country. He can tell us whether or not it is true that there is now ready an agreement formulated by the United States, with the full knowledge of the government of Canada, with respect to this matter.

I am not saying that is the case, but these are the indications we are receiving at every turn. We are entitled to know, before parliament adjourns, with respect to this very vital matter of whether or not the government has a policy; and if it has, the government should state it in a forthright and unambiguous way.

2140712,ca.proc.d.1961-09-13.36.1,1961-09-13,0daa460f-b2c1-447e-abbe-c4bd1f237b32,ca.m.6630,,,"SYDNEY, N.S.-USE OF LOW VOLATILE COAL FOR STEEL",,,"1.
column2: Has the Sydney, Nova Scotia, steel plant recently invited from the United States of America quotations for low volatile coal for blending purposes in the production of steel?
If so, what are the quantities of coal involved?
Does the low volatile coal required exist in the maritimes?
If not, what is the difference in the costs of making steel using low volatile coal imported

column1: from the U.S.A. and using the most suitable coal available in the maritimes?
Answer by: Hon. Paul Comtois (Minister of
Mines and Technical Surveys):

column2: This is a matter affecting the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation Limited and is not one of government responsibility. However, the press has reported the movement of one cargo of low volatile coal into Sydney for this purpose.
Since this is a matter of private business, the government has no official information.
No coal of low volatile rank is known to exist in the maritime provinces.
The government has no information on this matter.
